ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) gives immediate passive immunity after exposure, covering the virus until the vaccine induces active response. It is essential for preventing disease when given promptly.

sections.p: Rabies immunoglobulin is a pooled human antibody preparation that neutralises rabies virus at the wound site and in the bloodstream. It is part of post‑exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and is given before symptoms appear.
Rabies virus is a negative‑sense RNA virus of the Rhabdoviridae family. It travels from the bite wound along peripheral nerves to the central nervous system, causing fatal encephalitis.
b: No effective treatment once CNS involvement begins

sections.p: Transmission occurs via saliva from infected animals, usually dogs, bats, or wildlife. After inoculation, the virus replicates locally, then ascends the nerves to the brain.
b: Bite or scratch; mucous membrane contact

sections.p: Rabies is a fatal encephalitis with a classic incubation of weeks to months. Early symptoms are nonspecific; once neurological signs appear, mortality is near 100%.
Clinical diagnosis is based on history of exposure and symptom onset. Laboratory confirmation is rarely needed before PEP.
b: PCR of saliva or CSF; virus isolation; serology

t.b: Detects viral RNA at the wound; positive confirms exposure but not required for PEP
Shows immune response after vaccination; not used acutely

sections.p: PEP consists of thorough wound cleaning, passive immunisation with RIG, and a series of active vaccine doses. RIG must be infiltrated around the wound and given intramuscularly.

t.b: Reduces viral inoculum; essential before RIG
20 IU/kg; ensures adequate neutralising antibody at site

sections.p: Remember that RIG is only useful before symptom onset; once neurological signs appear, no therapy can reverse the disease. In low‑resource settings, prioritize wound care and RIG availability.
b: Give RIG within 24 hours of exposure

whenToSeekHelp: Any animal bite or scratch from a potentially rabid animal; exposure to bats; any wound that is deep, contaminated, or in a high‑risk area (face, hands).

faq.q: Can I use animal rabies immunoglobulin instead of human?
faq.a: No, animal products are not recommended; they lack standardisation and may cause adverse reactions.

faq.q: Do I need RIG if I already have a vaccine?
faq.a: Yes, RIG provides immediate passive protection; the vaccine alone is insufficient until antibodies develop.
Proceed with wound care and the vaccine series; the risk of disease increases but some protection remains.
